questions.prompt: The tree is `1` with left child `2` and right child `3`; `2` has children `4` (left) and `5` (right). What is its in-order traversal?
questions.explanation: In-order visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree: `4, 2, 5`, then `1`, then `3`. `1, 2, 4, 5, 3` is pre-order (node first), `4, 5, 2, 3, 1` is post-order (node last), and `1, 2, 3, 4, 5` is level order, which is BFS rather than DFS.

questions.prompt: Maximum Depth, Balanced Binary Tree and Diameter of Binary Tree all compute something at each node from its children's results. Which traversal order does that?

choices.text: Pre-order, because the root is visited first
In-order, because it visits nodes in sorted order
Level order, because it handles one level at a time
Post-order, because both children finish before their parent

questions.explanation: A node's height depends on its children's heights, so the children must be finished first: left, right, then the node. That's post-order, and it's what a recursive function does when it combines the return values of its two recursive calls. Pre-order suits passing information down, such as a depth or bounds. In-order's sorted order only matters for binary search trees.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between pre-order, in-order and post-order DFS, and name a problem from this lesson (or a common task) that suits each.

model_answer.summary: They differ in when the node itself is visited relative to its subtrees: before them, between them, or after them. Pre-order suits pushing information down or copying, in-order gives sorted order in a BST, and post-order suits values computed from children.
key_points: Pre-order: node, left, right; suits work done before the children, such as Invert Binary Tree (swap, then recurse) or copying a tree
In-order: left, node, right; on a binary search tree it visits values in sorted order
Post-order: left, right, node; suits values built from the children, such as height, balance or diameter
Same Tree can compare the two current nodes first, then recurse (pre-order style)
All three visit every node once: O(n) time and O(h) stack for a tree of height h

questions.explanation: The three orders are the same recursion; only the position of "visit the node" moves. Choose the order by asking whether the node needs its children's answers (post-order) or the children need the node's (pre-order).

questions.prompt:
What goes wrong with this Invert Binary Tree solution?

```python
def invert(root):
    if root is None:
        return None
    root.left = invert(root.right)
    root.right = invert(root.left)
    return root
```

choices.text: Nothing: it swaps the children correctly at every node
It inverts only the root and leaves the subtrees unchanged
Both children end up as the same subtree, and the original left subtree is lost
It recurses forever because `root.left` is reassigned before the second call

questions.explanation: The first line overwrites `root.left` with the inverted right subtree before the original left subtree has been saved. The second line then inverts `root.left`, which is now that same right subtree, so both children point to it and the original left subtree is unreachable. On `[2, 1, 3]` both children become the `3` node. Assigning both at once fixes it: `root.left, root.right = invert(root.right), invert(root.left)`. The recursion ends at `None`, so it doesn't loop.

sources.claim: Inverting mirrors the tree and returns its root; Example 2 turns [2,1,3] into [2,3,1].

questions.prompt: What is the maximum depth of the tree `[3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]` (root `3`, children `9` and `20`, and `20` has children `15` and `7`)?
questions.explanation: The problem defines maximum depth as the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. `3 → 20 → 15` has 3 nodes. The answer 2 counts edges instead of nodes. The recursion is `depth(None) = 0` and `depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right))`.

sources.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree - LeetCode
sources.claim: Maximum depth counts nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path; Example 1 `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]` has depth 3.

questions.prompt: An O(n) Balanced Binary Tree solution uses one recursive helper. What does that helper return for each subtree?

choices.text: The subtree's height, or a sentinel such as `-1` once any part of it is unbalanced
Only `True` or `False`, recomputing heights inside each call as needed
The number of nodes in the subtree
The diameter of the subtree

questions.explanation: Returning the height lets the parent check `abs(left - right) <= 1` without walking the subtree again. The `-1` sentinel carries "unbalanced" up the tree, so the check stops early. A helper that returns only `True` or `False` must call a separate height function at every node, which repeats work. Node counts don't decide balance: a tree is height-balanced when, at every node, the two subtree heights differ by at most one.

questions.prompt: Explain how to check whether a binary tree is height-balanced in O(n) time.

model_answer.summary: Use one post-order recursion that returns each subtree's height and checks the balance condition on the way up, returning a sentinel as soon as any node is out of balance. Each node is visited once.
key_points: Height-balanced means that at every node the left and right subtree heights differ by at most 1
A post-order helper computes the left and right heights first, then checks the node
It returns `1 + max(left, right)` when balanced, or `-1` as soon as any subtree is unbalanced
Each node is visited once, so O(n) time and O(h) stack space
Calling a separate height function at every node recomputes the same heights over and over

questions.explanation: Returning two things at once, the height and whether it's balanced, is a pattern that recurs in tree problems. Diameter uses the same idea, with a running maximum in place of the sentinel.

questions.prompt: What is the diameter of the tree `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` (root `1`, children `2` and `3`, and `2` has children `4` and `5`)?
questions.explanation: The problem measures the diameter in edges: the longest path between any two nodes. `4 → 2 → 1 → 3` has 3 edges. The answer 4 counts the nodes on that path instead. At each node the longest path through it is `height(left) + height(right)`, with heights counted in nodes.

sources.title: Diameter of Binary Tree - LeetCode
sources.claim: The diameter is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes, which may or may not pass through the root; [1,2,3,4,5] has diameter 3.

questions.prompt: Why isn't the diameter just `depth(root.left) + depth(root.right)` computed once at the root?

choices.text: The longest path may not pass through the root, so every node must be checked
That sum counts nodes, but the diameter is measured in edges
The root's own depth has to be added, giving one more
That formula takes O(n²) time, which is too slow

questions.explanation: The problem says the longest path may or may not pass through the root. If the root has only a deep left subtree that branches in two, the longest path lies inside that subtree. So the O(n) solution computes `left + right` at every node during one post-order pass, keeps the largest value seen, and returns `1 + max(left, right)` to the parent. The root-only sum is O(n), but it gives the wrong answer on such trees.

sources.title: Diameter of Binary Tree - LeetCode
sources.claim: The diameter is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes, which may or may not pass through the root; [1,2,3,4,5] has diameter 3.

questions.prompt: Explain the O(n) algorithm for Diameter of Binary Tree.

model_answer.summary: Do one post-order DFS that returns each subtree's height. At every node, `left + right` is the longest path through that node, so keep the largest one seen; that is the diameter in edges.
key_points: A helper returns the height of a subtree (0 for `None`, else `1 + max(left, right)`)
At each node, `left_height + right_height` is the number of edges on the longest path through that node
Keep a running best (an outer variable or `nonlocal`) and update it at every node
The answer is that best, measured in edges, and it may not pass through the root
Each node is visited once: O(n) time, O(h) stack

questions.explanation: The helper's return value (height) and the answer (diameter) are different things. Returning one while recording the other is the trick in this problem.

questions.prompt: In an iterative pre-order DFS with a stack (`node = stack.pop()`, visit it, then push its children), in which order must you push the children to visit left before right?

choices.text: Right child first, then left, because a stack returns the last item pushed
Left child first, then right, the same order as the recursion
Only the left child; the right child is visited on the way back
It doesn't matter, because a stack visits children in either order

questions.explanation: A stack is last in, first out, so the child pushed last is popped first. To visit left first, push right, then left. Pushing left first gives a right-to-left pre-order. A queue here instead of a stack would give level order (BFS).

questions.prompt: In CPython with default settings, what happens when you run a recursive DFS for Maximum Depth on a 10,000-node tree where every node has only a left child?

choices.text: It works, because Python grows the call stack as needed
It works, but takes O(n²) time
It raises `RecursionError`, because the default recursion limit is 1000
It crashes the interpreter with a segmentation fault every time

questions.explanation: A chain of 10,000 nodes needs 10,000 nested calls. CPython's default recursion limit is 1000 (`sys.getrecursionlimit()`), so it raises `RecursionError` (checked on 3.11 to 3.14). An iterative DFS with your own stack has no such limit. Raising the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` is possible, but the docs warn that too high a limit can crash Python.
